title: Adjacency Matrix
body:
One of the two ways to store a [[Graph]]: a $V \times V$ grid of booleans where
`M[i][j]` is true when there is an edge from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$. For a
[[Weighted Graph]] the cell holds the weight instead, with some sentinel (0 or infinity) for
"no edge".

```
      A  B  C  D
   A  0  1  1  0        A --- B
   B  1  0  1  0        |   /
   C  1  1  0  1        C --- D
   D  0  0  1  0
```

An undirected graph gives a matrix symmetric about the diagonal, since every edge is stored
twice. A [[Directed Graph]] does not.

## Cost

| | |
|---|---|
| Space | $O(V^2)$, regardless of how many edges there actually are |
| "Is there an edge from $u$ to $v$?" | $O(1)$, one array index |
| List all neighbours of $u$ | $O(V)$, you scan the whole row |
| Add or remove an edge | $O(1)$ |

The $O(1)$ edge test is the reason to use it, and the $O(V^2)$ space is the reason not to.
A graph with 10,000 vertices and 20,000 edges needs $10^8$ cells to store 20,000 facts.

**Use a matrix for dense graphs**, where $E$ approaches $V^2$ and the space is being paid
for anyway, or when the algorithm is constantly asking "are these two connected?".
**Use an [[Adjacency List]] for sparse ones**, which is most real graphs.
